design_detail: Retrospective comparative clinical series from one otolaryngology department (University of Brescia, Italy), January 1991 to December 1999: 18 people with cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions (CIMDL), 17 of whom admitted cocaine use at the first visit, compared with all 21 consecutive people with Wegener granulomatosis (WG) who had a nasal biopsy in the same department and period. Compared: symptoms and organ involvement, blood tests, ANCA (tested in three laboratories by immunofluorescence and several antigen-specific assays), CT or MRI read by one radiologist (16 people in each group), and nasal biopsies (44 from the CIMDL group, 29 from the WG group). Follow-up 12 to 108 months (median 34) in the CIMDL group; repeat imaging in 4 of them. No abstract: the paper ends with a summary.
can_establish: What the lesions looked like in 18 people treated for severe cocaine-related destruction of the nose at one Italian referral department (which structures were destroyed, what biopsies and blood tests showed, which infections occurred), and which features differed from 21 people with WG seen there in the same years, including how often routine ANCA tests were positive in each group.
cannot_establish: How common such lesions are among people who snort cocaine, or how often each structure is affected in milder cases (a referral series of severe cases with no denominator); whether amount or duration of use matters (history unreliable or missing for 7 people and never analysed); whether lesions stop or heal after stopping (the only repeat imaging was in 4 people who kept using); or how well each feature would tell the two diseases apart in an ordinary clinic (the predictive value comes from a sample with as many people with WG as with CIMDL).

sample.recruitment: Clinic: people evaluated in the Department of Otolaryngology of the University of Brescia between January 1991 and December 1999 (p. 391). The summary calls the CIMDL group consecutive (p. 403); the methods do not say how the 18 were identified. Controls: all 21 consecutive people with WG who had a nasal biopsy in the same department and period (p. 391).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: CIMDL: cocaine use with midline destructive lesions; no further criteria stated (p. 391). WG: biopsy-proven disease or the Chapel Hill consensus definition (p. 392).
sample.demographics: CIMDL: 10 men and 8 women, aged 22 to 66 (median 37; mean 35, SD 10). WG: 9 men and 12 women, aged 30 to 64 (median 45; mean 45, SD 14) (pp. 391–392; Table 1). Of the WG group, 19 were seen at first diagnosis and 2 at first relapse; 5 had kidney involvement, 3 disease limited to the nose and trachea, and 13 lung or other systemic involvement without kidney disease (p. 392).
sample.attrition: Follow-up 12 to 108 months (median 34) in the CIMDL group and 13 to 108 months (median 52) in the WG group (pp. 391–392); losses to follow-up not reported. Imaging in 16 of 18 people with CIMDL and 16 of 21 with WG; repeat imaging in 4 people with CIMDL (7 to 52 months after the first) (p. 392).
sample.selection_effects: A tertiary referral series of severe lesions, considered for a vasculitis diagnosis: every person with CIMDL had septal destruction and the group excludes milder damage such as an isolated septal perforation. The authors say referral bias may explain the differences from WG, because people with cocaine-related lesions may seek care only after substantial damage, while WG is often detected earlier through other organs (p. 400). Groups differ in age (mean 35 against 45).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at the first visit: 17 of 18 admitted cocaine use; reliable information on duration and amount could not be obtained for 7 (p. 391). No toxicology is mentioned.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Intranasal. Self-reported history (p. 391): 2 people used for 6 and 8 years, amount undetermined; 1 used 1 to 3 g a week irregularly; 8 used for 2 to 30 years at 1 to 15 g a week. These amounts are the participants' reported histories; they were not related to the lesions in any analysis.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Adulterants are mentioned only as a possible contributor to tissue damage (introduction, p. 391) and to ANCA formation (discussion, p. 402).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported at presentation. The 4 people with repeat imaging all said they had continued using cocaine (p. 396).

comparison.controls: 21 people with WG and nasal involvement who had a nasal biopsy in the same department and period (p. 391).
comparison.matching: None. The WG group was older (mean 45 against 35 years, p = 0.018) and had more women (12 of 21 against 8 of 18) (Table 1, p. 392).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a comparison between two diseases; for the CIMDL group, other drug use, earlier nasal disease or surgery, and timing of last use are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Cocaine or other drug use in the WG group is not reported. 13 of 21 people with WG were taking broad-spectrum antibiotics at diagnosis, so their nasal cultures were not done (pp. 393–394).

outcomes.instruments: Endoscopy with rigid 0° and 30° telescopes and a flexible scope, with archived images; blood counts, ESR, CRP, liver and kidney tests, urinalysis, hepatitis B and C and HIV serology, ANA, rheumatoid factor and complement; ANCA by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) and MPO and PR3 ELISA in Brescia, IIF and MPO ELISA at the Mayo Clinic, IIF on HMC-1 cells expressing PR3 or human leukocyte elastase (HLE), and PR3 capture ELISA; CT in 5 people (7 studies, without contrast) or MRI in 11 people (17 studies), all read by one radiologist, scoring 1 point per eroded structure and measuring septal perforation area (product of maximum diameters); biopsies with haematoxylin-eosin, elastic, fungal and mycobacterial stains, polarised light, immunostains (CD20, CD3, CD56, CD68) and Epstein-Barr virus studies (pp. 392–393).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability data for endoscopy, imaging or histology; one radiologist read all imaging (p. 392); blinding to group is not reported. ANCA assays followed published standard procedures, with the Mayo assays developed in one author's laboratory (p. 392).
outcomes.operationalization: A structure counted as involved if eroded or destroyed on imaging at presentation (Table 3); histological features were counted per biopsy (Table 4) and, for leukocytoclastic vasculitis only, also per person (p. 398).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p of 0.05 or less was taken as significant for all comparisons (p. 393). The count of 44 is approximate (editors' count: 13 comparisons with p values in Table 1, 10 in Table 3, 8 in Table 4 and about 13 more in the text).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for imaging or histology.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts, percentages and p values. Imaging at presentation, CIMDL against WG (16 each, Table 3, p. 398): septum 16 against 2; inferior turbinates 12 against 0 (both sides 9); middle turbinates 10 against 0 (both sides 5); superior turbinates 2; lateral nasal wall 5; lamina papyracea 1; hard palate (nasal floor) 4; soft palate 1; none of these beyond the septum in WG. Positive predictive value of septal perforation for CIMDL 88.9% in this sample (p. 396). Mean imaging score 4.06 (range 1 to 10) against 0.13 (0 to 1), p < 0.001 (p. 396). Editors' calculation, Wilson 95% intervals for the CIMDL shares: inferior turbinate 75% (50.5 to 89.8), middle turbinate 62.5% (38.6 to 81.5), lateral nasal wall 31.3% (14.2 to 55.6), nasal floor 25% (10.2 to 49.5). Blood (Table 1): CRP mean 12.2 against 79.4 mg/L, ESR 31 against 66 mm/h, haemoglobin 14.2 against 11.1 g/dL. ANCA positive by routine tests: 13 of 18 against 19 of 21 (p. 403). Biopsies (Table 4): leukocytoclastic vasculitis 7 of 25 against 14 of 22 biopsies (p = 0.02), but 6 of 18 against 9 of 21 people (printed p = 0.11; p. 398); giant cells or granulomas 0 of 25 against 9 of 22 and deep necrosis 0 of 25 against 19 of 22 (both p < 0.001).
analysis.selective_reporting: Exposure data were not analysed against the lesions. Figure 3's site percentages differ from the text and Table 3 (see reporting issues). Histology was analysed per biopsy, with up to 16 biopsies from one person, and per person only for leukocytoclastic vasculitis, where the per-biopsy difference disappeared. Table 3 gives both Yates-corrected and uncorrected chi-square p values for counts as small as 4 against 0, without saying which is used.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 16 to 18 people per group, shares have wide intervals (editors' Wilson intervals above), and a null difference between groups does not exclude a large one.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 people referred with severe cocaine-related nasal destruction, the septum was perforated in everyone and destruction often extended to the turbinates (inferior 12 of 16 imaged, middle 10 of 16), less often to the lateral wall (5) and nasal floor (4), and palatal perforations appeared in 5 people by the end of follow-up. Systemic illness was absent at presentation, inflammatory markers were on average much lower than in WG, routine ANCA tests were positive in 13 of 18, and biopsies shared vascular changes with WG but never showed the granulomas, giant cells or deep necrosis seen in WG. The 4 people re-imaged had all kept using cocaine and all had progressed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion says signs of systemic inflammation are “universally absent” in CIMDL (p. 402), and the discussion that laboratory tests showed no significant abnormalities (p. 400), but CRP was abnormal in 9 of 18 and ESR in 8 of 18, white cells were raised in 5 and anaemia was present in 2 (p. 393): lower than in WG on average, not absent. A centrifugal progression of necrosis from the septum outwards (p. 400) is inferred mainly from which structures were destroyed together at one time; repeat imaging exists for only 4 people, all still using. The 88.9% positive predictive value of septal perforation depends on this sample's equal numbers of imaged people with CIMDL and WG and would differ in a clinic with another mix. The statement that capture-ELISA negativity sets the cocaine-related ANCA apart from those in WG (p. 402) relies on a literature figure of under 5%, while Table 2 shows that 2 of the 13 WG sera tested by capture ELISA were also negative (editors' count). The authors do state that referral bias may explain the clinical and radiographic differences (p. 400) and that ANCA tests alone cannot separate the two diseases.

timeline.event: Trimarchi, Nicolai, Lombardi et al.: 25 people from the same group, with some data on progression over time (as tabulated by Nitro et al., 2022; not read; patients may overlap with this series).
Trimarchi, Bondi, Della Torre et al.: palatal perforation as a feature distinguishing CIMDL from granulomatosis with polyangiitis, 10 people (as tabulated by Nitro et al., 2022; not read).

Systematic review pooling 17 series (127 people), of which this series supplies 18 people and the largest set of detailed lesion and pathology data; septal involvement in all but one person across the series
Expert consensus: CIMDL diagnosis should not rely on autoantibody tests, which can be positive or negative (statement 1.3), consistent with this series' ANCA findings

replication.where_it_stands: The landmark comparison of cocaine-related midline lesions with WG. Its site pattern (septum always, turbinates often, palate and orbit less often) recurs across the series pooled by Nitro et al. (2022), but that pool includes this series and two later series from the same group, so independent confirmation is thinner than the pooled numbers suggest. The finding that routine ANCA tests are often positive is reflected in the 2025 consensus (statement 1.3). No later study read here followed people after they stopped using.

funding.funder: Dr. Russell's work was supported by training grant HL-07897; Dr. Specks' work was supported in part by grant AI-47572 from the National Institutes of Health (p. 391).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Brescia (otorhinolaryngology, nephrology, pathology, radiology) and the Mayo Clinic (pulmonary and critical care medicine; otolaryngology) (p. 391). Several ANCA assays (HMC-1 cells expressing recombinant PR3 or HLE) come from one author's research laboratory (p. 392). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre series of everyone presenting with cocaine-related nasal damage, from isolated septal perforation to extensive destruction, with toxicology, standard endoscopy and CT read blind by two radiologists, current ANCA testing, and repeat examinations in people who stop and people who continue using, would give how often each structure is affected, the course after stopping, and the accuracy of each feature for telling CIMDL from WG in an unselected clinic population.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: For people with severe cocaine-related lesions referred to specialist care, a tertiary department over nine years is a reasonable frame; for people who snort cocaine, or people with milder damage, it is not (no denominator; referral bias acknowledged, p. 400).

The summary calls the CIMDL group consecutive (p. 403) but the methods give no identification procedure or definition of a midline destructive lesion (p. 391); the WG controls were all consecutive biopsied patients.
18 people (16 imaged): enough to describe the range of damage, not to estimate how often each structure is involved with any precision (for example 75%, 95% interval about 50 to 90%).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Setting, period, age, sex, follow-up and blood tests are described; cocaine-use history is missing or unreliable for 7 of 18, and use at presentation and during follow-up is reported only for the 4 re-imaged.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Site shares come from 16 of 18 people with imaging; cultures from 17; ANA in 16, rheumatoid factor in 8, complement in 9 (Table 1). Biopsies cover all 18.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Endoscopy, CT or MRI and multiple biopsies are appropriate, but the cocaine attribution rests on self-report (one person did not admit use) without toxicology, and one radiologist read all images without stated blinding.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Imaging differed between people (CT in 5, MRI in 11), with most CT studies done at other hospitals (the methods say two of 5 CT studies were done in the department, although they count 7 CT studies in 5 people), and biopsies per person ranged from 1 to 16; no reliability data.

Shares are given without intervals; histology is compared per biopsy although one person contributed up to 16 biopsies, a difference that vanished per person; small counts were tested with chi-square rather than exact tests; and at least two printed p values could not be reproduced (sex, p = 0.037; vasculitis per person, p = 0.11).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: A clinical series, not a survey; missing imaging is covered under item 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI prevalence items are applied to a small comparative case series, as the round brief directs (case series: the JBI prevalence checklist). The clinical, imaging and histological observations appear careful, and the WG comparison group was consecutive, so what was seen in these 18 people is credible as observed. The risk lies in using the shares as frequencies: a referral sample of severe cases, unclear selection, imaging in 16 people with no reliability check, and statistics with several errors; the editors' summary is therefore high. Citable for: which structures were destroyed in these 18 people (septum in all, turbinates often, palate perforated in 5 by the end of follow-up), the absence of systemic illness and lower inflammatory markers than in WG, positive routine ANCA tests in 13 of 18, the histological features seen only in WG, infections in the destroyed nose, and progression in the 4 re-imaged people who kept using. Not citable for: how often snorting cocaine causes such damage, how often each structure is affected in general, the course after stopping, or the accuracy of any feature in practice.

key_findings.finding: 18 people with CIMDL (10 men, 8 women, aged 22 to 66, median 37) were seen in one Italian otolaryngology department from 1991 to 1999 and followed for 12 to 108 months (median 34). All but one admitted cocaine use at the first visit; reliable information on duration and amount could not be obtained for 7.
key_findings.locator: Patients and Methods › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 391); Table 1 (p. 392)

key_findings.finding: All came for longstanding symptoms including nasal obstruction, nosebleeds and severe facial pain. At the first visit the commonest findings were diffuse necrotising ulcers, extensive crusting and septal perforation; destruction of the septum and inferior turbinates was found clinically in all, extending in more severe cases to the middle and superior turbinates and lateral nasal wall, which was entirely absorbed in 3. Palatal perforations were present in 2 people at the first visit and appeared during follow-up in 3 more; the authors say the lesions gave rise to difficulty swallowing and nasal reflux (numbers not given).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical and laboratory findings, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The imaging data (p. 395) show inferior turbinate destruction in 12 of 16, not all; Table 1 records facial pain in 3 of 18. The paper says the lesions substantially affected quality of life without measuring it.

key_findings.finding: On imaging at presentation (16 people with CIMDL): septal perforation in all 16; at least partial destruction of the inferior turbinate in 12 (75%; both sides in 9); of a middle turbinate in 10 (62.5%; both sides in 5); erosion of the superior turbinates in 2; of the lateral nasal wall in 5 (31.25%; always the medial maxillary wall, reaching the lamina papyracea in 1); of the nasal floor in 4 (25%; reaching the soft palate in 1).

In the 16 people with WG imaged, septal perforation was seen in 2 (12.5%) and no other structure was eroded (16 of 16 against 2 of 16, p < 0.0005; positive predictive value of septal perforation for CIMDL 88.9% in this sample). Involvement of a second structure besides the septum occurred in 75% of the CIMDL group and in no one with WG; mean imaging score 4.06 (range 1 to 10) against 0.13 (0 to 1), p < 0.001. Clinically, all 21 people with WG had crusting, 3 a septal perforation, and none turbinate, lateral wall or palate involvement.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical and laboratory findings, 3rd paragraph (p. 393); Results › Radiographic findings, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 395–396)

key_findings.finding: Pattern: middle turbinate destruction occurred only in people who also had inferior turbinate involvement, and lateral wall or nasal floor involvement always went with inferior and middle turbinate involvement; the area of the septal perforation correlated with the number of structures eroded (r = 0.803, p < 0.001), and hard palate perforation with destruction of both inferior (r = 0.509) or both middle (r = 0.545) turbinates. The authors read this as a centrifugal spread from the septum outwards.
key_findings.locator: Results › Radiographic findings, 4th paragraph (p. 396); Discussion › Clinical and radiographic differentiation of CIMDL and WG, 1st paragraph (p. 400)

key_findings.finding: Repeat imaging was obtained in 4 people, all of whom said they had continued using cocaine; all showed progressive erosion. In one, over three years (1996 to 1999), destruction spread to the whole framework of the nose with complete erosion of the hard and soft palate and of the central anterior skull base, with a large meningoencephalocele. No repeat imaging is reported for anyone who stopped.
key_findings.locator: Results › Radiographic findings, 8th paragraph (p. 396); Fig. 2 legend (p. 395)

key_findings.finding: Infections: during follow-up 2 people with severe destruction developed orbital infections spreading from the nose (pseudotumour, bulging eye, double vision) and 1 a Staphylococcus aureus lung abscess; all resolved rapidly with antibiotics. 15 of 17 people with CIMDL tested at the first visit grew S. aureus from the nose. The authors state that chronic infection of the necrotic lesions is almost impossible to eradicate.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 footnotes (p. 392); Results › Clinical and laboratory findings, 2nd and 6th paragraphs (p. 393); Discussion › ANCA in CIMDL, 6th paragraph (p. 402)

key_findings.finding: Systemic features at presentation, CIMDL against WG (Table 1): fever 0 against 13, weight loss 0 against 7, joint pain or arthritis 0 against 7, lung involvement 0 against 12, ear involvement 0 against 7; haemoglobin 14.2 against 11.1 g/dL, CRP 12.2 against 79.4 mg/L (p = 0.002), ESR 31 against 66 mm/h (p = 0.009). Within the CIMDL group, CRP was abnormal in 9 and ESR in 8 of 18, white cells raised in 5 and anaemia present in 2; liver and kidney tests were normal and hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests negative in all.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 392); Results › Clinical and laboratory findings, 5th paragraph (p. 393)

key_findings.finding: Routine ANCA tests were positive in 13 of 18 people with CIMDL (8 P-ANCA and 5 C-ANCA by immunofluorescence) against 19 of 21 with WG. In the CIMDL group no serum reacted with MPO, all 5 C-ANCA sera reacted with PR3 in at least two assays, 5 of the 13 positive sera reacted with HLE and 4 reacted with two target antigens; in WG, reactivity matched the expected antigen in all but one person, none reacted with HLE and none with two antigens. Because of the positive ANCA, some people with CIMDL were first treated with cytotoxic drugs, to no avail.
key_findings.locator: Results › ANCA results, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 394–395); Table 2 (p. 397); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 400)
key_findings.note: The number of people given cytotoxic drugs is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Biopsies: of 44 biopsies from the CIMDL group, 19 showed only nonspecific fibrosis with mild inflammation or extensive necrosis, and 25 (57%) a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate: perivenulitis in 24 of 25, microabscesses in venule walls in 10, leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis in 7, and thrombi or scarred vessel walls in 7. Granulomas, giant cells and deep necrosis were found in none of the CIMDL biopsies but in 9 and 19 of 22 WG biopsies (p < 0.001); these extravascular changes were the only histological features that distinguished the two diseases. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis was commoner in WG per biopsy (7 of 25 against 14 of 22, p = 0.02) but not per person (6 of 18 against 9 of 21).
key_findings.locator: Results › Histopathologic findings, 1st to 5th paragraphs (pp. 397–398); Table 4 (p. 398)

key_findings.finding: Enlarged palatine or pharyngeal tonsils, often with small fluid collections, were seen on imaging in 9 of 16 people with CIMDL (56.25%) against 2 of 16 with WG (12.5%, p < 0.05); reduced or uneven enhancement of the mucosa of the septum and adjacent turbinates was more frequent in CIMDL (45.45% against 16.66%, p < 0.05).
At the time, the authors knew of only 24 published cases of CIMDL with adequate clinical and pathological documentation, and considered its incidence unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives p = 0.037 for the sex distribution (10 men and 8 women against 9 men and 12 women); the editors' Fisher exact test gives p = 0.53 (chi-square p = 0.43).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups do not differ significantly by sex; the printed p value is wrong, or belongs to another row.

reporting_issues.issue: The clinical results say destruction of the septum and inferior turbinates was found in all patients, while imaging found inferior turbinate destruction in 12 of 16 (75%), the figure repeated in the discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Clinical and imaging assessments differ, or the clinical statement is too broad; the imaging figure (12 of 16) is the one with a stated denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3 gives the CIMDL group septum 100%, inferior turbinate 61%, middle turbinate 33%, superior turbinate 16%, lateral wall 11% and floor or palate 28%, which do not match the imaging counts in the text and Table 3 (75%, 62.5%, 12.5%, 31.25% and 25% of 16) or the clinical statement that the inferior turbinates were destroyed in all; the values are close to counts of 11, 6, 3, 2 and 5 of 18, of which only the 28% matches a stated count (palate perforations in 5 of 18 at the first visit or during follow-up, p. 393); the rest are not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure understates inferior and middle turbinate and lateral wall involvement relative to the text (and slightly overstates the superior turbinate); claims should use the text and Table 3 with their denominator of 16.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says signs of systemic inflammation are universally absent in CIMDL and the discussion that laboratory tests showed no significant abnormalities, while the results report abnormal CRP in 9 and ESR in 8 of 18 people, raised white cells in 5 and anaemia in 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mild inflammatory changes were common; what differed from WG was their size and the absence of other organ involvement.

reporting_issues.issue: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis per person, 6 of 18 against 9 of 21, is given p = 0.11; the editors' Fisher exact test gives p = 0.74 (chi-square p = 0.54).
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion (no difference per person) stands; the printed p value cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is said to be more frequent in ANCA-positive than ANCA-negative people (41.6% against 20%, p = 0.6) without denominators; 41.6% corresponds to no whole number of the 13 ANCA-positive people (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the comparison is per person or per biopsy is unclear; the difference is in any case not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 shows that two C-ANCA-positive WG sera (WG 7 and WG 8, both positive on HMC-1/PR3 immunofluorescence) were negative in the PR3 capture ELISA: 2 of the 13 C-ANCA-positive WG sera tested by that assay (editors' count; 18 WG sera were tested by it in all); the discussion contrasts the 2 of 5 capture-negative C-ANCA sera in the CIMDL group with a literature figure of under 5% in WG without mentioning its own controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: In this sample, capture-ELISA negativity did not clearly separate the groups (editors' Fisher exact test, 2 of 5 against 2 of 13, p = 0.53).

reporting_issues.issue: 13 of 21 people with WG were on antibiotics and not cultured, and the text then refers to the remaining 7, which leaves one person unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the WG culture denominator is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Biopsies with nonspecific changes are given as 44% in the CIMDL group, whereas 19 of 44 is 43.2% (editors' arithmetic).
The correlation between septal perforation area and imaging score in WG (0.708, p = 0.002) rests on 16 people of whom only 2 had any perforation and whose scores ranged from 0 to 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The WG correlation is driven by two people and says nothing about a dose-like relation in WG.

reporting_issues.issue: Typesetting: the third WG patient is labelled WB 3 in Table 2; the chi-square column of Table 3 is headed with an aleph and every p value is printed with a less-than sign (including p < 1.000); serum creatinine is printed 1.01 + 0.4 in Table 1.
